title: Insults and Schemes as David Flees
overview: As David flees Jerusalem during his son Absalom's revolt, some people use his weakness to grab land, settle old scores or seize power, while one loyal friend slips into the rebel camp.

parts.label: Ziba's gift and accusation (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Ziba, who ran the estate of Saul's disabled grandson Mephibosheth, brings David welcome supplies and claims his master is hoping to win back Saul's throne. David gives Ziba the whole estate on the spot, but Mephibosheth later tells a very different story (chapter 19), and many readers suspect Ziba lied to get the land.

parts.label: Shimei curses David (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: Shimei, a man from Saul's clan, throws stones and calls David a murderer, saying the LORD is paying him back for deaths in Saul's family by handing the kingdom to Absalom. Earlier chapters present David as not responsible for those deaths, but to Saul's relatives he was still the man who took their family's throne.

parts.label: David refuses revenge (vv. 9-14)
parts.note: When his commander Abishai offers to behead Shimei, David says the LORD may be behind the curse and hopes God will see his misery and repay it with good. Many read this as David feeling the weight of his real wrongs, such as taking Bathsheba and having her husband Uriah killed, even though Shimei's particular charge was unfair.

parts.label: Hushai joins Absalom (vv. 15-19)
parts.note: Hushai is actually David's friend, sent back to Jerusalem to work against Absalom from the inside (chapter 15). He wins Absalom's trust by promising to serve the one the LORD and the people have chosen, and many readers see a quiet double meaning there, since David was also the LORD's chosen king.

parts.label: Ahithophel's shocking advice (vv. 20-23)
parts.note: Taking a king's concubines (secondary wives) was a public claim to his throne, so this act on the palace roof made the break with David final and showed Absalom's followers there was no turning back. The women had no say in it, and the scene matches the prophet Nathan's earlier warning that David's wrongdoing would bring public disgrace on his household (12:11-12).

disagreement: Readers differ on whether David's patience with Shimei is sincere humility before God or partly shrewd politics, especially since David later tells Solomon to have Shimei put to death (1 Kings 2).
think: When harsh criticism comes at your lowest point and is partly unfair, how do you tell what to dismiss from what might be worth hearing?
